title: Design Choices: Framework vs Code, Workflow vs Agent, Loops & Latency
scopeHtml: Scope: Choosing frameworks vs plain code, deterministic workflows vs agents, preventing loops and budgeting latency.

notes.title: Four design decisions that decide whether an agent ships
notes.html:
Before you write any agent code you make four choices, usually without noticing. Each one is cheap to get right on day one and expensive to fix on day ninety.

  1. Framework or plain code? Do you build on LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Spring AI, LangChain4j, or call the model API directly in your own code?
  2. Workflow or agent? Is the sequence of steps decided by YOUR code (a workflow) or decided by the MODEL at run time (an agent)?
  3. How do you stop loops? An agent that calls tools repeatedly can call the same tool forever, and every call costs money and time.
  4. What is the latency budget? Each model call takes seconds; an agent makes many of them in a row. Users wait.

Quick vocabulary, defined once:

  • LLM (large language model): a model that takes text in and produces text out. You call it over an API.
  • Token: a chunk of text (roughly three quarters of an English word). You pay and wait per token.
  • Tool call: the model replies "please run function X with arguments Y"; YOUR code runs it and sends the result back. The model never runs anything itself.
  • Agent loop: call model, run requested tools, append results, call model again, until the model answers without asking for a tool.
  • Workflow: a fixed pipeline you wrote (step A, then B, then C), where some steps happen to call an LLM.
  • Latency: how long the user waits. Budget: the most you allow yourself to spend (time, money, steps).

These four are linked. A framework makes it easy to build an open-ended agent, which makes loops likely, which makes latency unpredictable. A plain-code workflow does the opposite. Seeing the links is the senior skill. See also: 01_A1 (the agent loop itself), 03_G1 (guardrails and termination at a policy level). This note goes deeper on the engineering choices and numbers.

simple, predictable, fast, cheap                    flexible, unpredictable, slow, costly
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
 single call -> prompt chain -> router -> parallel -> orchestrator -> free agent
 (you decide every step)                             (model decides steps)

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "agents are the modern way, workflows are old" - the best production systems use the least autonomy that solves the problem.
  • Treating the four choices as independent; they compound (autonomy raises loop risk and latency variance).
  • Starting with a framework before you can describe the loop in ten lines of plain code.

notes.title: Framework vs plain code: what a framework actually gives you
notes.html:
A framework (LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, AutoGen in Python; Spring AI and LangChain4j on the JVM; vendor agent SDKs from model providers) is a library that gives you ready-made pieces for LLM apps. Verify current feature sets in each project's docs; they change fast.

What you typically get:

  • Provider adapters: one interface over Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible, Gemini, Ollama. Swapping a model is a config change.
  • Prompt templates and output parsers: fill variables into a prompt, parse JSON back into a typed object.
  • Tool plumbing: turn a function into a tool schema, dispatch the model's tool request to the function, feed the result back.
  • Memory and chat history helpers.
  • Retrieval helpers: document loaders, chunkers, vector store connectors (RAG pieces).
  • Orchestration: graphs/state machines with checkpoints, retries, human-in-the-loop pauses (LangGraph is the best-known Python example; verify details).
  • Observability hooks: tracing integrations (for example LangSmith, OpenTelemetry exporters).

What a framework costs you:

  • Indirection: when output is wrong you must find out whether the bug is your prompt, the framework's hidden prompt, or the parser. Some abstractions inject their own system text you did not write.
  • Churn: LLM libraries have changed APIs often; upgrades break code. Pin versions.
  • Lowest common denominator: a new provider feature (prompt caching controls, extended thinking, a new tool type) may not be exposed for weeks, so you drop to the raw SDK anyway.
  • Dependency weight and security surface: a large transitive tree to audit.
  • Learning two things: the model's behavior AND the framework's vocabulary.

What plain code looks like: the provider SDK (anthropic for Python, com.anthropic:anthropic-java for Java/Kotlin, or raw HTTPS) plus your own loop. For a basic agent that is about 30 to 60 lines. You own every prompt, every retry, every log line.

Real examples: Anthropic's public guidance on building agents recommends starting with direct API calls and only adding a framework when it clearly helps, noting frameworks can obscure the underlying prompts and responses (verify against the current guide). Teams often prototype in LangChain, then rewrite the hot path in plain code once behavior is understood. LangGraph is commonly picked specifically for durable state and resumable execution, not for tool calling, which is trivial.

Real life. A framework is a meal kit: fast to the first dinner, but when it tastes wrong you do not know which sachet is guilty. Plain code is cooking from ingredients: slower at first, but you taste every step.

Common interview traps.

  • "Frameworks are always bad" or "always good" - both are wrong; the answer is "what does it buy me that 40 lines do not?"
  • Forgetting that the framework hides prompts; you must log the final request actually sent.
  • Not pinning versions of a fast-moving LLM library.

notes.title: Framework vs plain code: a decision rule and the 40-line agent
notes.html:
Use this rule of thumb.

Situation Lean towards
One to three LLM calls, fixed order Plain code
You must debug exact prompts and tokens daily Plain code
Need to run on many model vendors quickly Thin adapter library, or an OpenAI-compatible gateway
Long-running flow that must pause, survive restarts, wait for a human Orchestration framework with checkpointing (or your own state in a database)
Standard RAG over documents with many connectors Framework retrieval pieces, plain code for the loop
Team is a Spring shop and wants DI, config, metrics consistency Spring AI or LangChain4j
Android app No agent framework on device; call your own backend

Questions to ask before adopting one:

  1. Can I write the loop in plain code in an hour? If yes, start there.
  2. Which exact feature do I need that I cannot cheaply write (checkpointing, tracing, connectors)?
  3. Can I see and log the real HTTP request?
  4. How often have its APIs broken in the last year?
  5. What is the exit cost if it is abandoned?

Here is the whole agent loop in plain code. It is deliberately small: that is the point. The helper call_model is your thin wrapper over the SDK (verify exact method names in the SDK docs); run_tool dispatches by name.

import os
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Current weather for a city.",
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["city"]},
}]

def run_tool(name, args):
    if name == "get_weather":
        return f"22C and sunny in {args['city']}"  # stub
    return f"error: unknown tool {name}"

def agent(question, max_steps=8):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for step in range(max_steps):                       # hard cap: no infinite loop
        resp = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
            tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
        results = []
        for b in resp.content:
            if b.type == "tool_use":
                results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                                "tool_use_id": b.id,
                                "content": run_tool(b.name, b.input)})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    return "Stopped: step limit reached."

print(agent("Is it sunny in Pune?"))  # prints the model's final answer
// Kotlin on the JVM: same loop; Kotlin uses the Java SDK. Verify exact builder
// and accessor names in the anthropic-java docs; the shape below is the point.
fun agent(question: String, maxSteps: Int = 8): String {
    val messages = mutableListOf<Msg>(Msg.user(question))   // Msg = your tiny wrapper type
    repeat(maxSteps) {                                      // hard cap
        val resp = model.call(messages, tools)              // wraps client.messages().create(...)
        if (!resp.wantsTool()) return resp.text()
        messages += Msg.assistant(resp)
        val results = resp.toolCalls().map { call ->
            ToolResult(call.id, runTool(call.name, call.args))
        }
        messages += Msg.toolResults(results)
    }
    return "Stopped: step limit reached."
}
// Prints the final answer, or the stop message after 8 model calls.
// Java: same loop with the anthropic-java SDK behind a small wrapper (verify names in docs).
static String agent(String question, int maxSteps) {
    List<Msg> messages = new ArrayList<>(List.of(Msg.user(question)));
    for (int step = 0; step < maxSteps; step++) {          // hard cap
        ModelReply resp = model.call(messages, tools);     // wraps client.messages().create(...)
        if (!resp.wantsTool()) return resp.text();
        messages.add(Msg.assistant(resp));
        List<ToolResult> results = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ToolCall c : resp.toolCalls())
            results.add(new ToolResult(c.id(), runTool(c.name(), c.args())));
        messages.add(Msg.toolResults(results));
    }
    return "Stopped: step limit reached.";
}
// Returns the final text, or the stop message after maxSteps model calls.

Notice what the plain version already contains: a step cap, an explicit message list you can log, and one place to add timeouts. A framework adds value only on top of this, not instead of understanding it.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming you need a framework for tool calling; it is a simple loop.
  • Ignoring Android: the on-device app calls your backend; the agent runs server-side so API keys never ship in the APK.
  • Building a bespoke orchestration engine when a checkpointing library or a database table would do.

notes.title: Workflow vs agent: the autonomy spectrum
notes.html:
Two words get confused, so define them precisely.

  • Workflow: the control flow lives in YOUR code. You decide that step 1 classifies the ticket, step 2 retrieves documents, step 3 drafts a reply. The model fills in the content of each step but cannot change the order.
  • Agent: the control flow lives in the MODEL. You give it a goal and tools; it decides which tool to call next, how many times, and when to stop.

It is a spectrum, not two boxes. Common workflow patterns, from simplest:

  1. Single call: one prompt, one answer. Often enough; try it first.
  2. Prompt chaining: output of step N is input to step N+1 (outline, then draft, then translate). You can insert a code gate between steps (check the outline has 5 sections, else retry).
  3. Routing: a cheap call classifies the input (billing, bug, sales) and your code sends it down a specialised path or a different model size.
  4. Parallelization: run independent calls at once (sectioning: split the task; voting: ask several times and compare).
  5. Orchestrator-workers: one model decomposes a task into subtasks at run time and delegates to worker calls. Already semi-agentic because the plan is dynamic.
  6. Evaluator-optimizer: one call writes, another critiques, loop until good or a cap is hit.
  7. Autonomous agent: open loop with tools, no fixed path.

This vocabulary matches publicly described patterns from Anthropic's agent-building guidance (verify the current wording). The point: every step to the right gains flexibility and loses predictability.

Workflow (you own the path):
 input -> classify -> [billing path | bug path | sales path] -> draft -> validate -> output
 Every arrow is code. Worst case = number of boxes x worst call time.

Agent (model owns the path):
 goal -> model -> tool? -> model -> tool? -> model -> ... -> answer
 Number of arrows is unknown before the run. Worst case = your step cap.

Why not just use agents everywhere? Because freedom has costs: more tokens (history grows every step), more latency, wider failure space, harder tests, harder security review. Why not workflows everywhere? Because some tasks truly have unknown paths: debugging an unfamiliar codebase, open-ended research, a support case where the next question depends on the last answer. Coding assistants such as Claude Code and Cursor-style agents use agent loops because the path through a codebase cannot be written in advance. A refund-approval or invoice-extraction pipeline in a bank is a workflow because the steps are known and auditable.

Real life. A workflow is a metro line: fixed stations, you know the arrival time. An agent is a taxi with a destination: more flexible, but the fare and time depend on traffic and the driver's choices.

Common interview traps.

  • Defining an agent as "anything that calls an LLM"; if your code fixed the order, it is a workflow.
  • Saying the evaluator-optimizer loop is safe without a round cap; it is a loop like any other.
  • Missing the middle: orchestrator-workers and routing give most of the benefit with bounded behavior.

notes.title: Workflow patterns in code: routing plus a gated chain
notes.html:
Here is a deterministic workflow with two LLM calls and a code gate. Control flow is ordinary if and for. Nothing here can loop forever, because there is no unbounded loop. Assume llm(prompt) is your thin wrapper returning text (verify the SDK call in docs).

import json

def llm(prompt: str, model="claude-haiku-5-5") -> str:
    ...  # thin wrapper over client.messages.create; returns the text of the reply

def handle_ticket(text: str) -> str:
    # Step 1: route with a cheap, fast model (small max_tokens keeps it quick)
    label = llm(f"Classify as billing, bug or other. Reply with one word.\n{text}").strip().lower()
    if label not in {"billing", "bug", "other"}:    # gate: never trust model output blindly
        label = "other"

    # Step 2: pick the path in CODE
    if label == "billing":
        context = lookup_invoice(text)              # plain function, no LLM
    elif label == "bug":
        context = search_known_issues(text)
    else:
        context = ""

    # Step 3: one bounded draft, then one bounded repair
    draft = llm(f"Reply politely.\nContext: {context}\nTicket: {text}", model="claude-sonnet-5-5")
    if len(draft) > 1200 or "TODO" in draft:        # deterministic quality gate
        draft = llm(f"Shorten and fix this reply:\n{draft}", model="claude-sonnet-5-5")
    return draft
# Returns a drafted reply; makes at most 3 model calls, ever.
fun handleTicket(text: String): String {
    var label = llm("Classify as billing, bug or other. Reply with one word.\n$text",
                    "claude-haiku-5-5").trim().lowercase()
    if (label !in setOf("billing", "bug", "other")) label = "other"   // gate

    val context = when (label) {                                      // path chosen in code
        "billing" -> lookupInvoice(text)
        "bug" -> searchKnownIssues(text)
        else -> ""
    }
    var draft = llm("Reply politely.\nContext: $context\nTicket: $text", "claude-sonnet-5-5")
    if (draft.length > 1200 || "TODO" in draft)                       // deterministic gate
        draft = llm("Shorten and fix this reply:\n$draft", "claude-sonnet-5-5")
    return draft
}
// Returns a drafted reply; at most 3 model calls.
static String handleTicket(String text) {
    String label = llm("Classify as billing, bug or other. Reply with one word.\n" + text,
                       "claude-haiku-5-5").trim().toLowerCase();
    if (!Set.of("billing", "bug", "other").contains(label)) label = "other";  // gate

    String context = switch (label) {                                         // path chosen in code
        case "billing" -> lookupInvoice(text);
        case "bug" -> searchKnownIssues(text);
        default -> "";
    };
    String draft = llm("Reply politely.\nContext: " + context + "\nTicket: " + text,
                       "claude-sonnet-5-5");
    if (draft.length() > 1200 || draft.contains("TODO"))                      // deterministic gate
        draft = llm("Shorten and fix this reply:\n" + draft, "claude-sonnet-5-5");
    return draft;
}
// Returns a drafted reply; at most 3 model calls.

Why this shape is production friendly:

  • Testable: you can unit test the router with 200 labelled tickets and measure accuracy. You cannot unit test "what will the agent do".
  • Cost known: worst case is 3 calls; you can price it per ticket.
  • Different models per step: a small model for the one-word classification, a larger one for writing. An agent with one model for everything cannot do this as cleanly.
  • Auditable: the path taken is a single label in a log line.

Parallelization is the other cheap win. If two steps do not depend on each other, run them at once (Python asyncio.gather, Kotlin coroutines async, Java CompletableFuture.allOf). Latency becomes the slowest of the two, not the sum. See also 01_A1 on parallel tool calls.

Common interview traps.

  • Letting the model output control a code path without validating it (the label not in set gate above).
  • Using the biggest model for every step including trivial classification.
  • Calling steps sequentially that are independent, doubling latency for no reason.

notes.title: Choosing: a decision procedure and the hybrid default
notes.html:
A practical decision order:

  1. Can one well-written prompt do it? Ship that. Add retrieval or examples before adding structure.
  2. Are the steps known in advance? Build a workflow (chain, router, parallel).
  3. Is it mostly known with one open-ended step? Hybrid: a workflow with a bounded agent inside that one step (for example "research" gets 6 steps and 3 tools; everything around it is fixed).
  4. Is the path truly unknowable and the stakes tolerable? Agent, with caps, budgets and approvals (see 03_G1).

Signals that push you toward an agent: the number of needed tool calls varies widely (1 to 30), the next action depends on discovered facts, the task is exploratory, and a wrong intermediate step is cheap and reversible. Signals to stay with a workflow: regulated or audited domain, strict SLAs, money or irreversible writes, a known process document already exists, a latency target under a few seconds.

Concern Workflow Agent
Latency Predictable (sum of fixed steps) Variable, often 3x to 10x more
Cost Predictable Grows with every step as history is re-sent
Testing Unit-testable per step Needs scenario evals, probabilistic
Failure mode A step returns bad output Loops, drift, wrong tool, compounding error
Debugging Read the path Read the whole trace
Flexibility Only what you coded Handles the unexpected
Security Narrow, fixed permissions Needs least privilege and gates

The cost point deserves a number. In a loop, each model call re-sends the whole conversation. Suppose the system prompt plus tools is 2,000 tokens and each step adds 500 tokens of tool output. Input tokens sent on call n is 2,000 + 500 x (n - 1). Over 10 calls: sum = 10 x 2,000 + 500 x (0+1+...+9) = 20,000 + 500 x 45 = 42,500 input tokens, versus 10 x 2,500 = 25,000 if history did not grow. Cost grows roughly quadratically in steps. Prompt caching (verify provider details) discounts the repeated prefix, but the growth shape remains.

Real products: Klarna-style support bots and bank KYC pipelines lean workflow; coding agents, deep-research products and computer-use agents lean agent. Many mature products are hybrids: a deterministic outer pipeline with agent steps inside.

Real life. Do not hire a consultant to decide each step of a task whose steps are written in the manual. Do hire one when nobody knows what is wrong with the machine.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking the agent because it demos better, ignoring that the demo is the happy path.
  • Forgetting that cost grows faster than linearly with steps because history is resent.
  • Giving one-line answers; interviewers want the decision criteria (known steps, stakes, SLA, auditability).

notes.title: Why agents loop: the failure patterns behind infinite loops
notes.html:
An infinite loop in an agent is rarely a literal endless while True. It is the model repeatedly choosing tool calls that do not move it forward. Because each iteration is a paid network call, a loop is both an outage and a bill.

Why models loop:

  • Same call, same result, no new information: the model searches "invoice 4412", gets empty results, searches again with the same words.
  • Ambiguous or unhelpful error text: the tool says "error" with no hint, so the model retries unchanged.
  • Oscillation: A fixes something and breaks B; fixing B breaks A (common in code-editing agents with failing tests).
  • No definition of done: the goal is vague ("make this better"), so the model never feels finished.
  • Tool output changes every time: a timestamp or random id in a result makes the model think the world changed.
  • Pagination traps: the agent keeps asking for "next page" of an endless feed.
  • Fan-out loops: a sub-agent spawns sub-agents.
  • Prompt injection: untrusted text tells the agent to keep going or to repeat an expensive action.
  • Context drift: after many steps the original instruction is far back in a long context and the model forgets it already tried something.

Typical symptoms in production: a single request with 40+ tool calls, a cost graph with a few runs far above the median, timeouts at the gateway while the backend keeps running, and one user retrying a stuck request making it worse (a retry storm).

Prevention is layered. No single guard is enough.

Layer Mechanism Catches
Hard step cap max_steps Everything, as the final backstop
Per-tool cap at most N calls to search Repeating one expensive tool
Duplicate detection hash of (tool, args); refuse repeats Same call, same args
Progress check no new facts in last K steps Wandering
Budget tokens, dollars, wall-clock Cost and time runaway
Circuit breaker disable a tool after M failures Flaky dependency
Informative errors tell the model what to do differently Blind retries
Termination design explicit finish tool or structured final answer Vague endings
Kill switch cancel a run by id Everything else

The most important design point: a guard that stops the loop must also tell the model or the user why. Silent truncation produces a half answer presented as complete. Return a structured stop reason ("step_limit", "budget_exhausted", "repeated_call") and what was achieved so far. See also 03_G1 (loops, runaway cost and termination) for the policy view; the next section is the code.

Real life. A person lost in a building who keeps turning right at the same corridor. A good guide gives a rule: "if you see this door twice, stop and ask for help".

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "set max_iterations" and stopping there; a cap alone ends the run but does not fix why it looped.
  • Retrying a failing tool call automatically N times inside the tool AND letting the model retry, multiplying attempts (N x M).
  • Forgetting that a client timeout does not cancel server-side work; you need cancellation.

notes.title: Loop prevention in code: duplicate detection, budgets, stop reasons
notes.html:
Below is a guard object you can drop into the plain-code loop from earlier. It enforces: a step cap, a per-tool cap, a wall-clock deadline, a token budget, and duplicate-call detection by hashing the tool name and arguments. When it refuses a call it returns text the model can read, which usually breaks the cycle ("you already did this, use a different approach or finish").

import hashlib, json, time

class LoopGuard:
    def __init__(self, max_steps=10, per_tool=4, deadline_s=30.0, max_tokens=60_000):
        self.max_steps, self.per_tool = max_steps, per_tool
        self.deadline = time.monotonic() + deadline_s
        self.max_tokens = max_tokens
        self.steps = 0
        self.tokens = 0
        self.seen = {}          # (tool,args hash) -> count
        self.tool_counts = {}

    def before_model_call(self):
        self.steps += 1
        if self.steps > self.max_steps:        return "step_limit"
        if time.monotonic() > self.deadline:   return "deadline"
        if self.tokens > self.max_tokens:      return "token_budget"
        return None

    def add_usage(self, input_tokens, output_tokens):
        self.tokens += input_tokens + output_tokens   # read from resp.usage (verify field names)

    def check_tool(self, name, args):
        key = (name, hashlib.sha1(json.dumps(args, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest())
        self.seen[key] = self.seen.get(key, 0) + 1
        self.tool_counts[name] = self.tool_counts.get(name, 0) + 1
        if self.seen[key] > 1:
            return "You already called this tool with identical arguments. " \
                   "Use different arguments, another tool, or give your best answer now."
        if self.tool_counts[name] > self.per_tool:
            return f"Tool {name} call limit reached. Answer with what you have."
        return None   # allowed

# In the loop:
#   stop = guard.before_model_call()
#   if stop: return {"status": "stopped", "reason": stop, "partial": last_text}
#   ... for each tool_use: msg = guard.check_tool(name, args)
#   result = msg if msg else run_tool(name, args)   # refusal is fed back as the tool result
import java.security.MessageDigest

class LoopGuard(
    private val maxSteps: Int = 10,
    private val perTool: Int = 4,
    deadlineMs: Long = 30_000,
    private val maxTokens: Int = 60_000,
) {
    private val deadline = System.nanoTime() + deadlineMs * 1_000_000
    private var steps = 0
    var tokens = 0
    private val seen = HashMap<String, Int>()
    private val toolCounts = HashMap<String, Int>()

    fun beforeModelCall(): String? {
        steps++
        return when {
            steps > maxSteps -> "step_limit"
            System.nanoTime() > deadline -> "deadline"
            tokens > maxTokens -> "token_budget"
            else -> null
        }
    }

    fun checkTool(name: String, argsJson: String): String? {
        val key = name + ":" + MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")
            .digest(argsJson.toByteArray()).joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it) }
        val repeat = seen.merge(key, 1, Int::plus)!!
        val total = toolCounts.merge(name, 1, Int::plus)!!
        if (repeat > 1) return "Identical call repeated. Try different arguments or answer now."
        if (total > perTool) return "Tool $name call limit reached. Answer with what you have."
        return null // allowed
    }
}
// Note: argsJson must be canonical (sorted keys) for the hash to match repeats.
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;

class LoopGuard {
    private final int maxSteps, perTool, maxTokens;
    private final long deadlineNanos;
    private int steps;
    int tokens;
    private final Map<String, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Integer> toolCounts = new HashMap<>();

    LoopGuard(int maxSteps, int perTool, long deadlineMs, int maxTokens) {
        this.maxSteps = maxSteps; this.perTool = perTool; this.maxTokens = maxTokens;
        this.deadlineNanos = System.nanoTime() + deadlineMs * 1_000_000L;
    }

    String beforeModelCall() {
        steps++;
        if (steps > maxSteps) return "step_limit";
        if (System.nanoTime() > deadlineNanos) return "deadline";
        if (tokens > maxTokens) return "token_budget";
        return null;
    }

    String checkTool(String name, String canonicalArgsJson) throws Exception {
        byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1").digest(canonicalArgsJson.getBytes());
        String key = name + ":" + HexFormat.of().formatHex(d);
        int repeat = seen.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);
        int total = toolCounts.merge(name, 1, Integer::sum);
        if (repeat > 1) return "Identical call repeated. Try different arguments or answer now.";
        if (total > perTool) return "Tool " + name + " call limit reached. Answer with what you have.";
        return null; // allowed
    }
}

Worked example. A model keeps calling search("invoice 4412"). Call 1 runs and returns nothing. Call 2 has the same hash, so check_tool returns the refusal text as the tool result. The model now sees "identical call repeated" and typically changes the query or answers. If it still repeats with a new argument every time, the per-tool cap (4) stops the bleeding at call 5, and the step cap (10) is the last wall.

Design details that matter:

  • Duplicate detection should be tolerant for idempotent reads only if cheap; for expensive or side-effecting tools (send, pay, create) a repeat should require explicit confirmation or an idempotency key so a retry cannot duplicate the action.
  • Count steps per model call, not per tool call, because parallel tool calls can pack many tools into one step.
  • Prefer cancellation tokens: a deadline checked only between steps cannot interrupt a 40-second tool call. Give every tool its own timeout (for example 10 seconds) in addition to the run deadline.
  • Make errors teach: "no rows found for customer_id=4412; valid ids look like C-1234" breaks loops far better than "error".
  • Add a finish or structured-output step so "done" is an explicit act, not an absence of tool calls.
  • Same loop in the app, not just the backend: a mobile client that retries a timed-out request while the backend still runs doubles the work; send a run id and make the endpoint idempotent.

Common interview traps.

  • Hashing arguments without canonicalizing key order, so {"a":1,"b":2} and {"b":2,"a":1} look different.
  • Making the cap huge ("just in case"); the cap should sit just above your p99 healthy run, found from traces.
  • Returning "error" and expecting the model to self-correct.
  • Refusing duplicates for legitimate polling (checking job status), which needs an explicit allowed-repeat rule with a delay.

notes.title: Agent latency budgets: where the time goes
notes.html:
Latency is the wall-clock time the user waits. A latency budget is the total you allow, divided into per-step allowances, like a financial budget: 8 seconds total means every step competes for that pool.

Why agents are slow: they are a chain of dependent network calls. The sum of the chain is the latency, and the chain length is not known up front.

Components of one model call (all approximate, vary by model and load; verify with your own measurements):

  1. Network and queueing: client to API and back, tens to hundreds of ms.
  2. Time to first token (TTFT): the model must read (prefill) the whole prompt before producing anything. Longer prompt means longer TTFT.
  3. Decode time: tokens are produced one after another. Time is roughly output tokens divided by tokens-per-second. A reply of 500 tokens at 50 tokens/second takes 10 seconds. That throughput figure is an illustrative assumption, not a promise from any provider.
  4. Tool execution time: your database, search API, or code sandbox. Often the largest unknown.
  5. Your own overhead: serialization, logging, auth, retries.

Per-step time is roughly TTFT + decode + tool. An N-step agent costs about N times that, and N is chosen by the model.

Worked example with explicit assumptions (illustrative, not measured):

Assumptions per step:
  network + queue        0.3 s
  TTFT (prefill)         0.8 s
  decode: 120 tokens at 60 tok/s = 2.0 s   (a tool-call turn is short)
  tool execution         0.9 s
  step total             0.3 + 0.8 + 2.0 + 0.9 = 4.0 s

A 5-step agent:  5 x 4.0 = 20 s
Final answer step: 400 tokens at 60 tok/s = 6.7 s decode + 1.1 s overhead = 7.8 s
Total ~ 4 steps x 4.0 + 7.8 = 23.8 s

User-facing target 8 s => this design is ~3x over budget.

To fix it you must decide which lever to pull. Each lever below is quantified against the example.

Lever Change Effect on the example
Parallel independent tool calls 2 of the 4 tool steps merge save ~ 4.0 s per merged step
Smaller, faster model for tool-calling turns decode 60 to 120 tok/s tool-turn decode 2.0 s to 1.0 s, saves ~1 s x 4 = 4 s
Shorter tool outputs less prefill and less context saves part of the 0.8 s TTFT growth
Streaming the final answer user sees first words after ~1 s perceived latency drops even if total is same
Caching tool results skip repeated 0.9 s tools saves up to 0.9 s per hit
Prompt caching of the stable prefix cheaper and faster prefill (verify provider support) lowers TTFT on every step
Fewer steps via better tools one get_customer_overview instead of 3 lookups removes whole 4 s steps
Workflow instead of agent fixed 2 calls 2 x 4 = 8 s

Notice that removing a step beats optimizing a step. A 4-second step deleted saves 4 seconds; shaving 10 percent off every step saves only 2.4 seconds here.

Real life. A relay race: the total time is the sum of every handoff and every leg. Making each runner a bit faster helps less than removing a leg.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting one latency number without separating TTFT, decode and tool time.
  • Optimizing the model while the slow part is your own database tool.
  • Forgetting that more context makes every later step slower (prefill grows).
  • Reporting average latency; users feel the p95 and p99, which for agents are dominated by long runs.

notes.title: Managing the latency budget in code
notes.html:
Treat time like the loop guard treats steps: a budget object that every step spends from and checks. Three techniques are shown together: a deadline passed to each call as a timeout, running independent tools in parallel, and a graceful degradation path (if time is nearly gone, stop planning and answer with what you have).

import asyncio, time

class TimeBudget:
    def __init__(self, total_s: float):
        self.end = time.monotonic() + total_s
    def left(self) -> float:
        return self.end - time.monotonic()

async def run_tools_parallel(calls, budget: TimeBudget, per_tool_s=5.0):
    # calls: list of (name, args); each gets min(per-tool limit, time left)
    async def one(name, args):
        timeout = max(0.1, min(per_tool_s, budget.left()))
        try:
            return await asyncio.wait_for(run_tool_async(name, args), timeout)
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            return f"error: {name} timed out after {timeout:.1f}s"   # model can see this
    return await asyncio.gather(*(one(n, a) for n, a in calls))

async def agent(question, total_s=8.0):
    budget = TimeBudget(total_s)
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for _ in range(6):
        if budget.left() < 2.0:                        # reserve time for the final answer
            messages.append({"role": "user",
                "content": "Time is almost up. Answer now using only what you have."})
            return await final_answer(messages, timeout=max(1.0, budget.left()))
        resp = await call_model_async(messages, timeout=budget.left())
        if not wants_tool(resp):
            return text_of(resp)
        results = await run_tools_parallel(tool_calls_of(resp), budget)
        messages += tool_messages(resp, results)
    return await final_answer(messages, timeout=max(1.0, budget.left()))
# Returns an answer within about total_s seconds, degrading instead of timing out.
import kotlinx.coroutines.*

class TimeBudget(totalMs: Long) {
    private val end = System.nanoTime() + totalMs * 1_000_000
    fun leftMs(): Long = (end - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000
}

suspend fun runToolsParallel(calls: List<Pair<String, String>>, budget: TimeBudget, perToolMs: Long = 5_000) =
    coroutineScope {
        calls.map { (name, args) ->
            async {
                val t = maxOf(100, minOf(perToolMs, budget.leftMs()))
                withTimeoutOrNull(t) { runToolSuspend(name, args) }
                    ?: "error: $name timed out after ${t}ms"          // visible to the model
            }
        }.awaitAll()                                                   // latency = slowest, not sum
    }

suspend fun agent(question: String, totalMs: Long = 8_000): String {
    val budget = TimeBudget(totalMs)
    val messages = mutableListOf(Msg.user(question))
    repeat(6) {
        if (budget.leftMs() < 2_000) {                                 // reserve final-answer time
            messages += Msg.user("Time is almost up. Answer now using only what you have.")
            return finalAnswer(messages, maxOf(1_000, budget.leftMs()))
        }
        val resp = withTimeout(budget.leftMs()) { callModel(messages) }
        if (!resp.wantsTool()) return resp.text()
        messages += Msg.fromTools(resp, runToolsParallel(resp.toolCalls(), budget))
    }
    return finalAnswer(messages, maxOf(1_000, budget.leftMs()))
}
// Returns within roughly totalMs, degrading to a best-effort answer.
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

class TimeBudget {
    private final long endNanos;
    TimeBudget(long totalMs) { endNanos = System.nanoTime() + totalMs * 1_000_000L; }
    long leftMs() { return (endNanos - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000L; }
}

static List<String> runToolsParallel(List<ToolCall> calls, TimeBudget budget, long perToolMs,
                                     ExecutorService pool) {
    List<CompletableFuture<String>> futures = calls.stream().map(c -> {
        long t = Math.max(100, Math.min(perToolMs, budget.leftMs()));
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> runTool(c.name(), c.args()), pool)
            .completeOnTimeout("error: " + c.name() + " timed out after " + t + "ms",
                               t, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);                 // Java 9+
    }).toList();
    return futures.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();      // latency = slowest, not sum
}

static String agent(String question, long totalMs, ExecutorService pool) {
    TimeBudget budget = new TimeBudget(totalMs);
    List<Msg> messages = new ArrayList<>(List.of(Msg.user(question)));
    for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
        if (budget.leftMs() < 2_000) {                                    // reserve final-answer time
            messages.add(Msg.user("Time is almost up. Answer now using only what you have."));
            return finalAnswer(messages, Math.max(1_000, budget.leftMs()));
        }
        ModelReply resp = callModel(messages, budget.leftMs());
        if (!resp.wantsTool()) return resp.text();
        messages.add(Msg.fromTools(resp, runToolsParallel(resp.toolCalls(), budget, 5_000, pool)));
    }
    return finalAnswer(messages, Math.max(1_000, budget.leftMs()));
}
// Returns within roughly totalMs, degrading to a best-effort answer.

Caveat: completeOnTimeout gives a fallback value but does not cancel the underlying work; the tool may keep running. For side-effecting tools use real cancellation (interruptible calls, HTTP client timeouts) as well.

More techniques used by real products:

  • Streaming (server-sent events): send tokens to the UI as they arrive. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini apps all stream, because perceived latency (time to first visible word) matters more than total time. For an agent, also stream status events ("Searching orders...") so a long run does not look frozen.
  • Tiered models: Haiku-class models for routing, extraction and simple tool turns; larger models for hard reasoning. Keeps most steps fast.
  • Speculative work: start a likely-needed retrieval while the model is still deciding (costs extra compute if wrong).
  • Async agents for slow work: if the task takes minutes, do not hold the HTTP request. Return a job id, run in a queue, notify by push/WebSocket (on Android, FCM or a poll). This is a product choice, not just an optimization.
  • Per-stage SLOs: budget table such as route 0.5 s, retrieve 1.0 s, generate 4 s, slack 2.5 s, so a regression points to a stage.

Real life. A trip itinerary with a fixed arrival time: you decide up front how long you spend at each stop and cut the last sightseeing stop if the train is close, rather than missing the train.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting only a global request timeout; a stuck first step then eats the whole budget with nothing to return.
  • Forgetting to reserve time for the final answer, so the run ends with a timeout instead of a best-effort result.
  • Parallelizing tool calls that depend on each other or share a rate limit.
  • Adding retries without including them in the budget, so a 5-second tool with 3 retries becomes 15 seconds.

notes.title: Production failure patterns and what to monitor
notes.html:
Put the four choices together and these are the incidents teams actually report. Check each against the controls above.

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Bill spikes on a few requests Loop with growing history Step cap, token budget, alert on cost per run
p50 fine, p99 is 90 s Long agent runs Deadline, degrade-to-answer, move long jobs async
Same tool called 12 times No duplicate detection, vague error Hash guard, informative errors
Agent "finishes" with a made-up answer after hitting the cap Silent truncation Return explicit stop reason and partial results
Duplicate emails or refunds Retry plus non-idempotent tool Idempotency keys, approval for side effects (see 03_G1)
Upgrade breaks behavior overnight Unpinned framework or silent model change Pin versions, golden-set evals before upgrade
Cannot reproduce a bad run No trace of prompts and tool args Log every request, response, tool call, latency, token counts per run id
Framework swallows an error Retries hidden inside the abstraction Log at the HTTP layer; count retries in the budget
Mobile users see spinner then error Backend run continues after client gives up Run ids, cancellation, async job pattern

What to measure per run, at minimum: steps, tool calls by name, input and output tokens, dollars, wall-clock per stage, stop reason (finished, step_limit, deadline, budget, error), duplicate-call refusals. Dashboards on the distribution of steps per run give an early signal: a rising p95 of steps means the model or a tool changed behavior. Set the step cap from this data, just above the healthy p99.

Rollout checklist for an agent that you choose to build:

  1. Confirmed a single call and a workflow were not enough.
  2. Plain-code loop first; framework only for named features.
  3. Step, tool, token and time caps with explicit stop reasons.
  4. Duplicate-call detection and informative tool errors.
  5. Per-tool timeouts, run deadline, cancellation.
  6. Latency budget per stage, p95 tracked, streaming for UX.
  7. Evals on a golden set including loop-prone scenarios; version pins.
  8. Approval gates and least privilege for side effects.

Real life. An aircraft cockpit: altitude, fuel and time are watched continuously and each has an alarm threshold, because by the time everything fails visibly it is too late to react.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing only prevention; interviewers also ask how you would detect and replay a bad run.
  • Alerting on average cost instead of per-run outliers.
  • Treating a hit cap as an error only; it is also data telling you the task or tools need redesign.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Four linked choices: framework or plain code, workflow or agent, loop control, latency budget. More autonomy raises loop risk, cost and latency variance.
  • Start with plain code. A basic agent loop is about 40 lines. Adopt a framework for a named feature (checkpointing, tracing, connectors, JVM DI integration), pin versions, and always be able to see the real request. Android apps call a backend; they do not host the agent or the keys.
  • Workflow means your code owns the path (chain, route, parallelize, gate); agent means the model owns it. Use the least autonomy that solves the problem; hybrids (a bounded agent inside a fixed pipeline) are common in production. Single call first, workflow next, agent last.
  • Agent cost grows faster than linearly because history is resent: in the worked example 10 steps send 42,500 input tokens versus 25,000 without growth.
  • Loops come from repeated identical calls, unhelpful errors, oscillation, vague goals, and untrusted instructions. Layer the defence: step cap, per-tool cap, duplicate-call hash, progress check, token and time budgets, circuit breakers, per-tool timeouts, explicit finish, kill switch. Feed refusals back as text and always return a structured stop reason with partial results.
  • Latency is the sum of a chain: network + TTFT + decode + tool + overhead, times the number of steps. Removing a step beats shaving every step. Levers: parallel independent tools, smaller models for easy turns, shorter outputs, caching, streaming, fewer and better tools, async jobs for long tasks.
  • Give every run a time budget with per-tool timeouts, reserve time for the final answer, and degrade to a best-effort answer instead of timing out.
  • Monitor steps, tokens, cost, per-stage time and stop reason per run; set caps from the healthy p99.
  • All latency figures here are illustrative assumptions; SDK method names and model ids should be verified against current docs.

Common interview traps.

  • Giving a single-technique answer (just max steps, just streaming, just a framework); strong answers name the trade-off and the layered controls.
  • Quoting precise provider speeds or prices from memory; say "measure and verify".
  • Forgetting the user: stop reasons, partial results and streamed status are part of the design, not afterthoughts.
